transcript.answer: Only partly. Sending the token as the WebSocket subprotocol keeps it out of the request line, so a URL-based access log won't capture it. The token is still sent in the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` request header. An ingress log with header capture, a proxy trace, or a debug log of the request can therefore still record it. The original documented claim of avoiding log exposure was 'only half true'. Issue #150 found that the server also echoed the token in the 101 response headers and kept it on the socket object. The fix, in HAL Engine 0.3.0, has the client offer `hal.v1` beside the token, and the server answers only `hal.v1`. The token no longer appears in any response header or on the socket's `protocol` property. The issue also requires that no offered subprotocol value is written to any log, and that the docs list every place the credential exists so operators can configure log redaction. Operators still need to redact the request header. A subprotocol value must be a valid HTTP token, so padded base64 tokens can't use this carrier.
sources: issue-150 (re-cinq/Otto #150: Stop echoing the access token in the WebSocket handshake response)

judgements.reason: The answer says the approach is not fully safe because the server echoed the token in the 101 response headers, and it describes the fix in which the client offers hal.v1 alongside the token and the server selects hal.v1, which matches the gold answer.
